To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of NHP bush meat samples were found to be infected with either SIV or STLV, 2) the prevalence of infection with SIV and/or STLV varied according to species, 3) new SIV and STVL lineages were identified and 4) the geographic distribution of the SIV and STL lineages identified in our study was restricted to the DRC.
we found a high prevalence of STLV and a wide genetic diversity in non-human primates bushmeat, and that we identified three new subtypes of STLV-1 in the Democratic Republic Congo.
(1) SIV and STLT are prevalent in bushmeat in rural areas of the DRC, and (2) new SIV and STTL variants were identified in bushmeat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential risk of zoonotic transmission of retroviruses to human populations, especially in rural areas where the hunting of NHP is still a major source of food.
the identification of new SIV and STLT strains in NHP in rural areas of DRC and the estimation of their prevalence in the NHP bushmeats.
a better understanding of the origin and spread of HIV and HTLV, and with the development of strategies for their prevention and control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DRC is a hot spot of simian retroviral infections, and that the DRC should be considered as a region of high risk of simian retro-virus cross-species transmission to humans.
the DRC remains a region with an important risk of cross-specie transmissions of simian retrovirus to humans.
SIV and STLVs are still present in NHP bushmeats, that their prevalences vary according to species, geographic region, and season, and that they represent a risk of zoonotic transmissions to humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified 6 new SIV and 4 new STLV strains in NHP from the DRC, and that SIV and STL infection rates in NHP bushmeats are still high in rural areas of the DRC.
we found high prevalence and diversity of retroviruses in non-human primate bushmeat in rural areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
SIV and STL-V1 are highly prevalent in NHP bushmeats and that new SIV and STVL-1 lineages have been identified.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an urgent need for more extensive surveys of simian retrovirus infections in NHP in Africa, especially in areas where NHP are hunted for food.

we should not underestimate the risk of cross species transmission of simian retrovirus from non-human primmates to humans, and that the risk may be even higher than what we know so far from our limited knowledge on the genetic and geographic diversity of these viruses.
the DRC is an important reservoir for simian retrovirues, with high diversity and high prevalences.
